summary: This article examines how sleep affects athletic performance and recovery, drawing on interviews with sleep researchers, physiotherapists, a nutritionist, a tech expert, coaches, a sports psychologist and a soccer player. It covers sleep science, recovery hormones, sleep needs, nutrition, tracking technology, routines, team and school settings, and travel-related disruption. The consensus is that sleep is a nonnegotiable pillar of health and athleticism.
one_line: Experts and athletes explain why sleep is as vital as training for sports performance, recovery, and injury prevention, with practical strategies.
key_facts: Dr. Julianne Hart, a sleep researcher, was interviewed on 15 September 2023 and said the literature on sleep and performance is 'unequivocal'.
Sleep has several stages, including Rapid Eye Movement (REM) and Non-REM sleep, and REM sleep is where much of the mental consolidation occurs.
Semi-professional soccer player Tyler Reynolds slept badly before the 2023 season opener on 2 September due to nerves and had less energy, slower reaction time and poorer mental sharpness.
After the bad game, Tyler Reynolds began treating his sleep schedule as seriously as his training regimen.
Sports physiotherapist Alicia Montoya said human growth hormone, vital for tissue repair and muscle growth, is released during deep sleep.
Alicia Montoya said insufficient sleep can lower motivation, increase perceived exertion and raise injury risk because fatigued muscles may not support joints adequately.
General advice for average adults is 7-9 hours of sleep per night, while Dr. Michael Thompson said athletes may need 9 to 10 hours depending on training intensity and physiology.
Nutritionist Sarah Lin said magnesium, found in green leafy vegetables and nuts, promotes better sleep, and advised athletes to avoid heavy meals close to bedtime.
Tech expert Jason Patel showed sleep-tracking devices on 12 October that capture sleep duration, quality and sleep stages.
Dr. Hart recommends a consistent bedtime and wake time, even on weekends, and reducing screen time before bed to limit blue light exposure.
Alicia Montoya suggests meditation or deep-breathing exercises to calm the nervous system and promote sleep.
Coach Daniel Becker said his team tries to synchronize sleep habits, especially before big games.
High school coach Christine Yang said teenagers need even more sleep and that her team educates students on its athletic and academic benefits.
Sports psychologist Dr. Eric Newman uses cognitive-behavioral strategies such as mindfulness and sleep scheduling before and during travel to counter stress and time-zone disruption.
